items.title: Joe Temperley interviewed by Monk Rowe, Aspen, Colorado, October 11, 1997
items.q: I used to go every Wednesday to hear Vic Dickinson because his

ctx.x: Well blues has got to be a part of the jazz music. And I was interested in hearing the second set last night, that they opened up with a blues tune. And it was really nice, just to hear some wailing.

You know I mean I think a lot of the trouble today is that the playing becomes too homogenized. Too many people sound alike. But you know I’m very interested in golf, and that’s what’s happening with golf too, because people go to golf school and they all come out with the same swing and they all look the same and they all play the same, they all play the same way. And for instance in the old days you could tell a musician by his vibrato. Ben Webster had a different vibrato completely to Lester Young or Coleman…

style was so personal. Playing out the side of his mouth and play all those beautiful things that he used to play, but it was so personal and so real. And that band, with Roy Eldridge and Prez and Vic Dickinson, sounded amazing. And they were three completely identifiable people. Conte Candoli said, “that can only be Little Jazz.”
